title: {{NAME}} and the Fairy Who Fixed the Machine
moral: Magic and science are just two different ways of solving the same problems.
character_anchor: Bright children's book cartoon illustration, bold outlines, vivid flat colours. {{NAME}}, a young boy with brown hair and blue eyes, wearing a bright copper-orange shirt, silver-grey overalls, and sturdy work boots — same child, same face, same exact outfit in every image.

pages.content:
The old mill on the edge of town had been broken for twenty years.

The gears were rusted, the waterwheel was stuck, and every engineer in the county had looked at it, shaken their head, and left.

{{NAME}} had read about the mill in a history book. He visited one afternoon with his toolkit.

When he reached the main gear mechanism, he found someone already there: a fairy, about the height of a matchstick, sitting inside the gear assembly with her sleeves rolled up.

pages.content:
Her name was Cogsworth, which she said was entirely her own idea and nobody else's business.

She had been trying to fix the mill for three years, she explained, but fairy magic was excellent at organic things (wood, water, living things) and less reliable on iron and steel.

"I can do the metal," said {{NAME}}. "If you can do the water intake, the sluice is completely jammed with something I can't reach."

Cogsworth looked at him appraisingly. "You'll have to do what I say."

"You'll have to do what I say too," said {{NAME}}.

She considered this. "Fine."

pages.content:
They divided the work precisely.

Cogsworth sent golden threads of magic through the wooden parts of the sluice mechanism, coaxing warped planks back into shape, convincing blocked channels to flow again.

{{NAME}} cleaned and oiled the iron gears methodically, removing rust flake by flake, checking each tooth, replacing three that had cracked.

They talked while they worked. Cogsworth had opinions on gear ratios. {{NAME}} had opinions on sluice angles. They argued productively for several hours.

pages.content:
At four o'clock, with the last gear cleaned and the last plank eased into place, {{NAME}} opened the water gate.

For a moment nothing happened.

Then: the water came. The wheel turned. The gears caught, one by one, the sound of the mill filling up from silence into a deep, rhythmic hum.

Cogsworth landed on the top of the wheel and rode it all the way around once, both arms out, completely triumphant.

{{NAME}} watched from the bank and felt the kind of joy that only comes from fixing something that was broken.

pages.content:
Cogsworth said goodbye at the mill door as the light turned golden.

She left him a gear no bigger than a thumbnail, made of a material that wasn't quite metal and wasn't quite wood, warm in his palm.

"For the next broken thing," she said.

That night, {{NAME}} put the tiny gear on his windowsill and watched it catch the last light.

Across town, the mill turned steadily in the dark. He could hear it if he opened his window: the sound of something fixed, doing its work, going on and on.
